claims.text: Rapid flash heating and cooling can produce noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Rapid post-heating cooling induces transient supersaturation in these nanoparticles.
Transient supersaturation produced by rapid cooling kinetically traps a metastable single-phase solid solution.
During rapid cooling, atomic diffusion is too limited for equilibrium phase segregation.
Slowing the cooling rate increases atomic mobility and the time available for diffusion.
The enhanced diffusion associated with slower cooling enables phase separation.
The enhanced diffusion associated with slower cooling enables elemental segregation.
Diffusion-driven phase separation under slower cooling produces secondary crystal phases.
Compared with the rapid-cooling baseline, reduced cooling rates will increase phase segregation and observable elemental segregation.
Compared with the rapid-cooling baseline, reduced cooling rates will lead to the appearance of additional crystal phases.
The proposed mechanism is applicable specifically to noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and processed by flash heating and cooling.
The cooling-rate threshold for the transition from kinetic trapping to segregation varies with composition and elemental diffusion coefficients.
